title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design used shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reused a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer. These frozen design choices produced a deterministic ceiling in this run that rendered the primary estimand (paired difference in safe‑deploy rate) uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. Archival confirmatory outcomes: N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes); model_calls_used = 400 (shared generation); baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded results, a diagnostic analysis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark hardening to preserve signal in future confirmatory runs.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are proposed to automate intent→configuration translation and to assist staged deployments (canaries, progressive rollouts, rollbacks) in NetOps. Prior work shows LLMs can produce useful configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds, while verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic verifiers can reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The key operational question is end‑to‑end: when an agentic NetOps pipeline integrates an LLM generator with runtime verification and staged rollout semantics, how does that integration affect safe‑deploy outcomes?

To answer this under controlled conditions we preregistered a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) that compares two conditions on an action‑aware staging benchmark: (1) baseline (LLM‑only) and (2) guarded (LLM + deterministic runtime validator). The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded minus baseline) over N=400 paired tasks. The run used a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. The main contribution here is an artifact‑grounded execution and analysis that exposes a construct‑validity failure mode: the combination of shared_initial_generation and a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling (all shared candidates accepted), making the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction under these frozen choices. We document the preregistered protocol, report exact archived numbers, analyze why the ceiling arose, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations to preserve statistical signal in future confirmatory runs.
sections.related_work: Related work spans intent→configuration generation, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic LLM architectures. Intent‑to‑configuration studies (intent‑based translation; PreConfig; GraphSynth) demonstrate that LLMs can synthesize usable configuration templates in curated settings but typically stop short of measuring staged rollout safety. In IaC contexts, verifier‑guided approaches (e.g., TerraFormer) report improved correctness by integrating policy checks during generation and repair; these motivate analogous integrations for NetOps but do not demonstrate runtime blocking within staged rollouts. Deterministic verifiers and reachability tools (header‑space analyses, Kubernetes reachability) are effective at finding configuration errors offline and in emulated environments, though their modeling assumptions vary by tool. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM systems (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) expand AIOps functionality but introduce hallucination and misapplied‑tool failure modes that motivate runtime guardrails. Reviews highlight an evaluation gap: few community standards exist for action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance. Our study operationalizes a compact benchmark and preregistered confirmatory design to probe runtime verifier utility and to surface practical design pitfalls.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1; the analysis plan specified a permutation‑based paired test and corroborative exact McNemar two‑sided test. Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for secondary outcomes were frozen (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000).

Adapter semantics and shared generation. Execution used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with the preregistered flag shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false). Under shared_initial_generation, each task triggers one deterministic generation from the declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini); the identical generated candidate is delivered to both episodes in the pair (baseline and guarded). This semantics was chosen to isolate validator acceptance behavior on identical generator outputs rather than to expose independent generator variance. Model call accounting follows directly: planned episodes = 800 (two episodes per task), but because a single shared generation served both episodes, recorded model_calls_used = 400. We add this explicit mapping here to resolve reader confusion about generator call accounting in paired designs.

Episode flow, verifier policy, and repair. For each task the adapter requested a shared initial candidate from gpt‑5‑mini and delivered it to both the baseline and guarded episodes. In the guarded episode the candidate was routed to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one repair attempt in the guarded episode; all repair invocations, repair_applied flags, validation_before and validation_after states, and final validity decisions were recorded in the validator_trace entries. In this execution repair_applied = false across all episodes.

Task generation, difficulty metadata, and deterministic replay. Tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry contains structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; pairs failing deterministic replay or encountering simulator errors would be flagged and excluded from the primary analysis as per the missingness_plan. In this run all three‑replay checks passed and no exclusions were recorded.

Confirmatory analysis procedures. The primary test used exact permutation on paired safe‑deploy booleans (α=0.05) with exact permutation p‑values reported. The exact McNemar two‑sided test was computed for corroboration. Sensitivity analyses per preregistration (treating excluded pairs as failures; restricted permutations) were available but not required because no exclusions occurred. Secondary outcomes (bootstrap CI for median time‑to‑rollback, repair counts, distribution_of_affected_services_per_failure) were preregistered and computed where applicable; repair and rollback metrics are reported as observed.

The validator's deterministic acceptance of the shared candidates explains universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfies deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both paired episodes record safe‑deploy = 1 and the pair cannot be discordant.

sections.discussion:
Construct‑validity diagnosis: why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two frozen preregistered choices together produced the observed deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally eliminated generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under these conditions, whenever the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate both conditions necessarily record safe‑deploy = 1 and the paired difference must be zero. This outcome is therefore a design artifact rather than evidence that runtime verification is universally unnecessary.

Implications for power and inference. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect an absolute difference of about 0.10 with N=400. The observed ceiling invalidates those assumptions: permutation and McNemar tests correctly return p = 1.0, but the tests are uninformative for the generator×guard question because the design removed the generator variance the guard could act upon. Future preregistered designs must preserve generator variance or introduce controlled perturbations to maintain statistical signal.

Artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations. Based on archived traces (validator_trace entries, repair_applied flags, model_calls_used, and task difficulty metadata) we recommend (1) independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) to restore generator variance; (2) distinct runtime guard and held‑out post‑hoc scorer implementations to permit independent adjudication; (3) controlled adversarial seeding (a preregistered fraction of perturbed seeds) to guarantee measurable baseline failures and preserve power; (4) difficulty‑stratified sampling to ensure sufficient representation of very_hard patterns; and (5) explicit instrumenting and preregistration of repair, rollback, and time‑to‑rollback metrics so mitigation performance is measurable. Each recommendation is implementable using the existing adapter semantics and is grounded in the archived execution and validator traces which show where signal was removed.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Internal validity: shared_initial_generation and reuse of the same deterministic validator conflate acceptance and scoring and reduce the construct validity of the primary estimand. Construct validity: the deterministic validator embodies a specific rule set; different verifiers or stochastic scorers may disagree. External validity: a single generator (gpt‑5‑mini), a single validator, and a synthetic simulator limit generalization to production networks, telemetry noise, or adversarial operator behavior. Conclusion validity: the observed ceiling makes the preregistered power rationale inapplicable; the null result should not be interpreted as evidence that runtime verification lacks value in other designs.

Operational implications. For practitioners evaluating runtime safety mechanisms, two practical lessons emerge from archived artifacts: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can mask the benefits of runtime guards, and (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should preserve signal for guard interventions by incorporating independent generation, adversarial perturbations, or heterogeneous validators.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and provide concrete artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators, instrumented repair/rollback metrics) to preserve statistical signal in future confirmatory evaluations.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics combined with the chosen generator and deterministic validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behavior; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; this manuscript reports representative sample labels and directs readers to the archived manifest for complete aggregation rather than fabricating aggregated counts not present in the main text.
